title: Lensing and enhanced single atom detection via a single-pixel nanostructure
authors: Ling-Xiao Wang, Lei Xu, Ai-Ping Liu, Guang-Jie Chen, Yuan-Hao Yang, Jia-Qi Wang, Xin-Biao Xu, Guang-Can Guo, Chang-Ling Zou, Guo-Yong Xiang
abstract: We propose and demonstrate a general mechanism for nanoscale lensing based on the phase gradient imposed by a single nanostructure scattering light in its near-field. We verify this effect using an optical waveguide on a substrate, with single atoms serving as quantum probes that sample the near-field intensity through their fluorescence. This quantum probing technique provides a unique, non-destructive approach to characterizing focused optical fields and reveals a 4-fold enhancement in single atom detection efficiency. This work establishes on-chip nanostructures as a multi-functional quantum optics platform that can efficiently route photons, localize fields, and enhance atom-photon coupling, offering new opportunities for trapping and manipulating single atoms and realizing hybrid nanophotonic-atomic systems for quantum applications.
summary: This paper demonstrates a novel mechanism for nanoscale lensing using integrated photonic waveguides. By employing single atoms as quantum probes, the researchers successfully measured a fourfold enhancement in single-atom fluorescence detection efficiency. This establishes on-chip nanostructures as a versatile platform for hybrid quantum applications.
main_problem: The research aims to develop an efficient method for loading and probing single atoms in the near-field of integrated nanophotonic devices.
main_result: The authors demonstrated a fourfold enhancement in single-atom detection efficiency by utilizing a nanoscale lensing effect induced by a single nanostructure.
method: The experiment involves using cold $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ atoms transported near a dielectric waveguide, where the fluorescence collection light path is modulated by the nanolensing effect.
model_or_system: The physical system is a hybrid photonic-atomic setup using an on-chip GaN waveguide and single neutral atoms. The core mechanism is nanoscale lensing, modeled by the phase gradient imposed by the nanostructure.
key_observables: Counts ratio $C(\Delta)$ quantifying collection modulation, and the measured single-atom detection probability.
important_parameters: Beam waist ($w_0$), Rayleigh length ($R$), and the enhancement factor (4-fold).
main_assumptions: The quadratic approximation for phase accumulation is used, and the fluorescence collection efficiency correction factor $\zeta(x)$ is approximated as unity.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the lensing effect schematically, the experimental setup involving MOT and waveguides, and plots comparing measured counts ratios with and without the nanolensing modulation.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from theoretical modeling of the lensing effect to experimental implementation using atom transport and fluorescence measurement, culminating in the quantitative demonstration of enhanced single-atom detection.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the interface between quantum optics and solid-state photonics, providing a practical platform for enhancing atom-photon coupling and enabling advanced quantum sensing.
